explanations.explanation: Micah, a prophet of the LORD, asks the leaders, "Should you not know justice?" (Micah 3:1). Look at who he's asking: the rulers, the very ones in charge. If I ran a bakery and didn't know what an oven was, I'd have bigger problems than a blurry stamp. Those in charge are the ones you'd expect to know it best.

Wealth never comes up in Micah's question. He asks the leaders of Jacob and the rulers of Israel, "Should you not know justice?" (Micah 3:1). Being in charge and knowing what's right are two different things, and he's pointing at the second one.

Micah doesn't ask about warfare here. His question to the leaders is, "Should you not know justice?" (Micah 3:1). It's a question for people who are supposed to guide others, and it sets up everything he says next.

Close, friend, but Micah says it the other way around. He tells the leaders, "You hate good and love evil." (Micah 3:2). These are the rulers he just asked, "Should you not know justice?" The text says hate for good and love for evil.

Right, because Micah says the reverse. The leaders "…hate good and love evil." (Micah 3:2). He's speaking to the people who are supposed to guard what's right. Instead, the text says they've got the two backwards.

Micah says, "Then they will cry out to the LORD, but He will not answer them." (Micah 3:4). It's a heavy line, and it comes right after the harm he described in the verses before. The text says plainly that the answer will be silence.

explanations.answer: He will answer them right away
explanations.explanation: The text says something different. Micah says they will cry out to the LORD, "…but He will not answer them." (Micah 3:4). I wish I had a happier answer to hand you on this one, friend. Micah describes a time when the cry goes up and no answer comes.

explanations.answer: He will send them a new king
explanations.explanation: A new king never shows up in this verse. Micah says, "Then they will cry out to the LORD, but He will not answer them." (Micah 3:4). I know a new king sounds like a tidy ending, but the text sticks to one thing: no answer.

Yes, and the text gives the reason. Micah says, "At that time He will hide His face from them because of the evil they have done." (Micah 3:4). It's the same stretch of verses where he said they hate good and love evil. The reason comes straight from the verse.

It's true, friend. Micah says, "At that time He will hide His face from them because of the evil they have done." (Micah 3:4). The verse names the evil as the reason. So the text is clear about what's behind the hidden face.

The LORD says these prophets "…declare war against one who puts nothing in their mouths…" (Micah 3:5). They proclaim peace while they chew, and the war goes to the one who gives them nothing. I've been in kitchens with more honest signals than that.

Blessing isn't what the verse says. The LORD says these prophets "…declare war against one who puts nothing in their mouths…" (Micah 3:5). The word is war. The prophets who lead His people astray give out peace to some and war to others.

Mercy doesn't show up here. The LORD says these prophets "…declare war against one who puts nothing in their mouths…" (Micah 3:5). That's the opposite of mercy. The text puts war against the one who gives them nothing.

Not quite, friend. Micah says the opposite: "Then the seers will be ashamed and the diviners will be disgraced." (Micah 3:7). No honor is handed out here. Ashamed and disgraced is how the text describes them once the visions are gone.

Correct, no honor is handed out. Micah says, "Then the seers will be ashamed and the diviners will be disgraced." (Micah 3:7). That comes after night falls over them without visions (Micah 3:6). Shame and disgrace are what the text gives them.

explanations.answer: There is no answer from God
explanations.explanation: The verse gives the reason itself. The seers and diviners "…will all cover their mouths because there is no answer from God." (Micah 3:7). A seer with nothing to see has nothing left to say. You know when everybody in the meeting turns to you for the answer and you've got NOTHING? That's the hand over the mouth.

explanations.answer: The leaders ordered them to be quiet
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says they "…will all cover their mouths because there is no answer from God." (Micah 3:7). No leader walks in, no order comes down. Nobody has to snatch the microphone from these guys, friend. They step up, find out there's no answer from God, and set it down all by themselves.

explanations.answer: They are afraid of the angry crowds
explanations.explanation: No crowds show up in this verse. Micah says they "…will all cover their mouths because there is no answer from God." (Micah 3:7). The text gives one reason, and it isn't about fear of a crowd. It's the silence from God.

Micah says, "…I am filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage…" (Micah 3:8). That's the 'however' after all the silence in the verses before. The seers will have no answer from God, and Micah has the Spirit of the LORD. His power comes from there, not from his own muscles, which in my case would be a relief.

The priests aren't his source. Micah says he is filled with power "…by the Spirit of the LORD…" (Micah 3:8). Later he says that Jerusalem's priests teach for a price (Micah 3:11). So the power comes from the Spirit, not from them.

The king's court never comes up in this verse. Micah says, "…I am filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage…" (Micah 3:8). No royal backing, no palace connections. And good thing, because the rulers of Israel are exactly who he's calling out in this passage. Try telling off your boss when your boss is the one signing your paycheck!

Micah says he's filled "…to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin." (Micah 3:8). That's a tough message to deliver, and it takes courage to say it. The text names what he declares: transgression and sin.

That's not Micah's message. He says he's filled "…to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin." (Micah 3:8). Peace is what the prophets who lead people astray proclaim (Micah 3:5). Micah says something different.

Victory isn't the message here. Micah says he is filled "…to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin." (Micah 3:8). He doesn't promise a win, he tells them their sin. The text puts it that plainly.
Micah says they are the ones "…who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with iniquity." (Micah 3:10). The building materials are the problem. That's a shaky foundation, friend.

Micah says the opposite. The leaders despise justice, and they are the ones "…who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with iniquity." (Micah 3:10). Honesty and fairness aren't the materials named here. The text says bloodshed and iniquity.

Prayer and praise aren't in this verse. Micah says they "…build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with iniquity." (Micah 3:10). Those are hard words to hand the leaders of a city, friend. Micah doesn't soften them one bit.
Yes, Micah says, "…her priests teach for a price…" (Micah 3:11). Teaching, with a price tag stuck right on it. It's there in his list with the leaders and the prophets. He names all three.

It's true, friend. Micah says, "Her leaders judge for a bribe, her priests teach for a price, and her prophets practice divination for money." (Micah 3:11). The priests are right there in the middle of the list. The text says they teach for a price.

explanations.answer: The LORD is among us so no disaster can come
explanations.explanation: They say, "Is not the LORD among us? No disaster can come upon us." (Micah 3:11). Notice that Micah says they lean upon the LORD even as they judge for a bribe and teach for a price. Bribes and all, and they STILL say no disaster can come. Micah's very next words say otherwise.

explanations.answer: The LORD has left us so disaster is coming
explanations.explanation: They don't say that. Micah says they lean upon the LORD, saying, "Is not the LORD among us? No disaster can come upon us." (Micah 3:11). I think they sound confident, not worried. They say He is among them.

explanations.answer: The LORD is far away so we can do as we like
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say. Micah says they lean upon the LORD, saying, "Is not the LORD among us? No disaster can come upon us." (Micah 3:11). They say He is among them, not far away. They also say no disaster can come.

explanations.answer: It will be plowed like a field
explanations.explanation: Micah says, "Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field…" (Micah 3:12). He pictures Zion plowed like a field. I think that's a hard picture to take in. Micah says it's because of them.

explanations.answer: It will be rebuilt with gold
explanations.explanation: That's not in the verse. Micah says, "Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field…" (Micah 3:12). Nothing here is rebuilt or made golden. The text says plowed, like a field.

explanations.answer: It will be ruled by Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't mentioned in this verse. Micah says, "Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field…" (Micah 3:12). The text doesn't name who rules it. It says what happens to Zion: plowed like a field.

Not quite, friend. Micah says, "…Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple mount a wooded ridge." (Micah 3:12). The temple mount is named in the list of what's coming. No spared place is mentioned in the verse.

Right, the temple mount isn't spared. Micah says, "…Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple mount a wooded ridge." (Micah 3:12). Even the mount where the temple stands is named. That's a sobering line, and the text doesn't soften it.
